content.title: Trump’s sanctions strategy against Iran has loopholes – and China is not the only one
content.lead: The U.S. wants to bring about the economic collapse of the Iranian regime. This is unrealistic. China is unlikely to allow it. And Tehran will hardly capitulate, no matter how great the pressure may be.

content.caption: Trump believes the regime in Tehran is collapsing. But it is not yet that far.
content.author: Imago

content.text: Undoubtedly, the balance of power in the Middle East has shifted somewhat in favor of the U.S. again in recent weeks. Along the Omani coast, the U.S. Navy has apparently succeeded in establishing a corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships can pass at night under U.S. military protection. The transport volume is probably significantly below pre-war levels, but oil prices have fallen below 90 dollars per barrel again. This allows U.S. President Donald Trump to maintain the naval blockade against Iranian ports indefinitely for the time being.

In August, Iranian oil deliveries to China plummeted by more than 60% compared to the previous year, as Reuters reports. Food prices in Iran recently rose by about 130%. Leading figures of the regime also admit to the economic problems. President Masud Pezeshkian declared on Friday that Tehran should end the war while it was still in a position of «strength and dignity.» Parliament Speaker Mohammed Ghalibaf, for his part, said: «Regardless of our military strength, we cannot survive if people are hungry and we have no economic growth.»

As the United Arab Emirates imposed a complete trade embargo against Iran last week, the regime's economic situation is deteriorating further. Tehran imported a large part of its goods via the Emirates and used their financial system to circumvent sanctions.

Now the U.S. government wants to further tighten the regime's economic isolation. Even before Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the intensified sanctions on Monday, he promised Iran an «economic D-Day» – in other words, the beginning of the regime's downfall. Bessent asserted that with «the greatest financial offensive» of all time, the U.S. would now usher in «the endgame» against Iran. He added that any country that still maintained economic ties with Tehran would be excluded from American financial markets. On Truth Social, Trump already triumphed on Monday: «The Iranian regime is collapsing completely.»

But it is not yet that far. Bessent did not announce any concrete punitive measures against specific countries on Monday. While some Chinese companies and individuals were on the expanded sanctions list, no major banks were. This indicates that Trump does not want to risk a major conflict with Beijing. In the trade dispute, he already had to make concessions to China after it restricted the export of rare earths to the U.S. and the import of U.S. soybeans.

China buys more than 80% of Iranian oil exports. It is thus the most important lifeline for the Iranian regime. Beijing threatened Washington on Tuesday with countermeasures should the U.S. implement its sanctions threats. A spokesman for the Chinese Foreign Ministry said that cooperation with Iran was based on international law. He added that Beijing did not accept «illegal, unilateral sanctions» and would defend its interests and rights. Already in February, the Chinese government had instructed five refineries processing Iranian oil to ignore U.S. sanctions.

Interestingly, Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to visit Washington on Sept. 24. Should Trump be unable to extract any concessions from him regarding Iran, the U.S. sanctions threats would definitely prove hollow.

However, the U.S. sanctions strategy has another drawback. It assumes that the regime must either collapse under pressure or be willing to make concessions it has previously rejected. Specifically, these would be the abandonment of the nuclear program, the handover of highly enriched uranium, a restriction of the missile program, renouncing the financing of foreign militias, and free passage through the Strait of Hormuz. But that is wishful thinking. Tehran is now convinced that Trump's ultimate goal is to overthrow the regime. Why should it give up precisely those armament programs and instruments of power intended to protect it from further U.S. attacks in the future?

Cornered, the regime is more likely to risk a new military escalation rather than capitulate in negotiations. Tehran would probably have little to fear. With the return to an economic sanctions strategy, Trump has signaled that he no longer wants a military escalation for the time being. Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh warned on state television on Monday: «Our defense is no longer so defensive. The enemies should expect an attack.»

On Tuesday morning, a tanker was again hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz. In the Red Sea, a ballistic missile from the pro-Iranian Houthi militia also struck a Saudi ship on Monday. The escalation spiral in the Middle East has not yet come to a standstill. And Trump has not yet found a solution to stop it.

newestTopComments.text: With all due respect: It's incredibly easy to pick out the weaknesses in Trump's strategy and write pseudo-intellectual articles about them. The crucial question, however, is: Who knows a smarter strategy than Trump – and which journalist will write a brilliant article about it?

Christian Weisflog describes one version of the China dilemma, but only draws the analytical conclusions in a fragmentary way: ♦ China wants cheap oil and doesn't want to be drawn into a war with Iran. ♦ Iran wants time, to save face, and to maintain its deterrent. ♦ Trump wants a visible victory and is working towards a regional Gulf power that keeps Iran in check. Weisflog's warning about China is one aspect. And the crucial question is not whether Iran will «capitulate,» but rather what degree of impoverishment of the civilian population or weakening of the Iranian elites is necessary for Tehran to seek a ceasefire.

metadata.nzzSummaryEN:
- The US is tightening sanctions against Iran to economically isolate the regime, but China remains a crucial obstacle as it continues to purchase Iranian oil.
- Despite mounting economic pressure and issues in Iran, Tehran shows no signs of capitulating; military escalations may increase.
- Trump's strategy is hindered by China's influence and the absence of concrete sanctions against major Chinese banks.
